newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav economy faces experiment in election year.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav economy faces experiment in election year.

text.p: Yugoslavia faces the challenge of pursuing a controversial expansion of the money supply while keeping prices and the dinar stable ahead of elections in September, economists said on Monday.

"Yugoslavia has been subject to an experiment with stabilisation applied to a comatose economy and forecasts based on experience, logic and reason are impossible," Dusko Susnjar, Yugoslav representative of the Vienna-based EPIC (European Privatization and Investment Corporation), said.
"This is an experimental laboratory situation to which economic theory is looking forward," Susnjar told Reuters.
Economists said monetary expansion allowed the ruling Socialists to pay wage and pension arrears ahead of Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections set for September 21.

But some financial analysts felt the tactics were irresponsible with the government spending much of what it had gained from selling a 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija in June for almost $1 billion.

It has extended half of the funds in the form of cheap, short-term credits to export industries, agriculture and infrastructure but analysts said some hard currency receipts ended in the state budget to plug holes and pay arrears.

"Whatever is going on is something we have certainly not desired. Dinars are printed with hard currency backing but it results in higher wages and consumption," said Slobodan Milosavljevic of the IZIT Institute for Market Research.
"One creates a positive picture but the effects will be short-lived. This consumption will increase to create an illusion of a better life but the costs will be high," he said.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) says it is committed to allowing the key M1 monetary aggregate to rise only by the overall economy's growth rate, forecast to reach 13 percent in 1997.
Yugoslavia's M1 money supply expanded to 6.5 billion dinars ($1.07 billion) at the end of June from 5.9 billion in May. M1 money supply stood at 5.234 billion dinars in January.

Despite the sharp growth in M1, the dinar and prices have remained stable. The dinar's black market rate hovers around 3.6 to the German mark and consumer price inflation slowed to 18.2 percent year-on-year in June. Annual inflation in 1996 reached 57.8 percent.
Analysts said monetary expansion began in June after the launch of a new 100-dinar banknote which coincided with the sale of the Telekom Srbija stake.
But Susnjar said the government behaved rationally, adding: "With the existing financial resources, any real push for development is impossible."
Economists felt that the government had no particular, long-term economic strategy apart from keeping the dinar stable and trying to ensure victory in the elections.
"The stable dinar rate is their crucial test and the point measuring success, because the currency rate has a special psychological importance for Yugoslavs," Susnjar said.
Yugoslavs vividly recall hyper-inflation which hit the country in 1993, amidst war in neighbouring Bosnia and Croatia and international isolation, with daily inflation running at 60 percent.
Analysts did not expect hyper-inflation to return but declined to forecast the economic situation after the election, with some of them hoping for little change.

"Despite accumulated problems, this is a closed system which functions. I believe they would retain the status quo, tackling the mounting problems on a case-by-case basis, with prices and the dinar remaining stable," Susnjar added. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
